text: and the use of pancreatic grafts from young donors who may be more resistant to a diabe- togenic effect.9 One possible alternative to complete pancreatic transplan- tation is an islet-cell graft. These have rarely been success- ful,1 with insulin independence at 1 year3 only in about 10% of cases. However, the use of carefully prepared islet cells from more than one donor and a modified immuno- suppressant protocol12 has produced greatly improved re- sults. In this ‘Edmonton Protocol’, corticosteroids were completely avoided because of diabetogenic effects. In- duction therapy with daclizumab was used, followed by maintenance with sirolimus and low-dose tacrolimus.12 Short-term follow-up data indicated that patients with un- stable type I diabetes benefited in terms of glucose control from islet transplantation.13 Reported insulin independ- ence was 80% at 1 year after use of the ‘Edmonton proto- col’14 and 10% at 5 years post-transplant.15 Thus, engraft- ing an adequate beta-cell mass appears to be the critical factor for transplant success.8 Insulin independence has been reported with single organs from cadaveric donors.16 Further study of the ‘Edmonton protocol’ confirmed that islet-cell transplantation may successfully restore endog- enous insulin production and glycaemic stability in pa- tients with type I diabetes mellitus. Insulin independence is gradually lost again in most cases, but persistent islet function without insulin independence confers benefit in terms of glycaemic control, provided the patient can toler- ate the immunosuppressive regimen. Islet transplantation may be best for highly selected patients with severe hy- poglycaemia or labile type I diabetes mellitus, provided all other attempts to stabilise glycaemic control have been tried. For patients seeking long-term insulin independ- ence, whole pancreas transplantation is a better option at present.17 See also under Diabetes Mellitus, p.431. The induction of tolerance,3,5,10,18 the possibility of neo- genesis of beta cells from pancreatic stem or precursor cells,10,18,19 less toxic immunosuppressive therapy, and en- hanced islet engraftment17 remain focuses of investigation in islet transplantation. 1.
